narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Dance references in Jewish history date back to the Bible and Talmud, which contain over 30 distinct dance terms.

During the dispersion, national community dancing ceased until the halutzim (pioneers) of the First, Second, and Third Aliyahs (1882–1923) reintroduced dances brought from the Diaspora, establishing the horah as the national dance.
Choreographer Rivka Sturman created over 90 dances between 1942 and 1983 to provide children with indigenous cultural reflections.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Created to help build a new Israeli culture and celebrate the pioneering spirit, dances are performed at life-cycle events like weddings and bar/bat mitzvahs, holiday celebrations such as Shavuot, and regular weekly recreational sessions.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Ensemble ADAR-KRAMIM (https://archive.org/details/EnsembleAdar-kramim_958)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances feature fixed choreographies matched to specific musical pieces selected by a yotzer (choreographer).
Formations include circles, couples, trios, short lines, and group line formations.
Movement is highly varied, incorporating the Tza'ad Temani, Horah, and dabke.
Watch for Tza'ad Temani, Horah.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Rivka Sturman created over 90 classic Israeli dances between 1942 and 1983.
Gurit Kadman organized the first Shavuot dance pageant and folk dance festival at kibbutz Dalia in 1944.
Influences include the European Hora, Hasidic dance traditions, the Middle Eastern Arabic dabke, and Yemenite steps.
Rooted in Diaspora folk dances brought by pioneers (including the horah, polka, Krakowiak, Czerkassiya, and rondo) combined with Middle Eastern and Jewish religious dance traditions.

scenes.title: Family tree
